gbs333-aD60.summary: The prologue to Book I is Biel's abridgment of Ockham's prologue, examining the epistemic status of theology. After a preamble that states the aim of theology (a savoring, charity-increasing knowledge of God), names Ockham as principal guide, and outlines three inquiries (theology as knowledge, its unity through its subject, and its practical or speculative character), the twelve questions proceed in three groups. The first group (qq. 1–8) concerns theology as knowledge. Q. 1 lays the epistemological foundation: it defines the wayfarer, evident knowledge, and theological truth, and develops Ockham's theory of intuitive and abstractive cognition and of apprehension and judgment. It concludes that God by absolute power can make some theological truths evident to a wayfarer, but not those requiring intuitive vision of God. Q. 2 defines scientific knowledge and the knowable proposition, sets out the divine distinctions and the distinct and indistinct concepts of God, and concludes that every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is demonstrable, against Scotus's ordering of divine rationes. Qq. 3–6 are briefer logical questions on attributes and their subjects (real distinctness, demonstrability of attributes of first subjects, definition as middle term, per se modes), carrying an Ockhamist semantics of abstract and connotative terms. Q. 7 concludes that theology as acquired under the common law is not science properly so called: its principles are believed, all theological habits except faith are open to an unbeliever, and the subalternation analogy fails. Q. 8 holds that acquired theology is an aggregate of specifically distinct habits, individuated by acts, while infused faith is one habit. The second group (q. 9) rejects Scotus's account of the subject of a science as virtually containing all its truths: the subject of a science is simply the subject of its conclusions, so theology has many subjects, of which God, Christ, or 'things and signs' may each be called first under different orders of primacy. The third group (qq. 10–12) treats praxis and practical knowledge. Praxis is any operation in the will's power, primarily acts of will, and is not really distinct from speculation. Practical and speculative knowledge are properly distinguished by their objects (conclusions directive of free action or not), with prudence differing from moral science as experience from doctrine. Theology contains both simply practical and simply speculative knowledge. Throughout, Biel follows Ockham against Scotus and Aquinas, engages Pierre d'Ailly and Gregory of Rimini, and stresses divine absolute power, ontological parsimony, and the limits of the wayfarer's knowledge of God.
claims: Theology as possessed by wayfarers under the common law is not science properly so called, because its principles are believed rather than evident, though God could by absolute power make some theological truths evident.
Contingent theological truths whose evidence requires intuitive vision of God cannot be made evident to a wayfarer; in this life we have only indistinct (common or composite) concepts of God.
Every necessary, doubtful, mediate proposition about God is in principle demonstrable.
Acquired theology is an aggregate of many specifically distinct habits rather than one habit; infused faith is one habit.
The subject of a science is just the subject of its conclusions; theology therefore has many subjects, and Scotus's virtual-containment account is rejected.

Praxis is any act in the will's power and is not really distinct from speculation; theology contains both practical and speculative knowledge, distinguished by whether its conclusions direct free action.
concepts: distinct vs. indistinct concepts of God

gbs333-aD2349.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I treats God's presence in creatures. The preamble summarizes Lombard's text in three conclusions: God is in all things by essence, presence, and power, more excellently in the saints by the grace of adoption, and most excellently in Christ by the grace of union. He is everywhere without change, circumscription, or limitation. And he remains in himself non-local and atemporal, independent of creation. The single question then examines the general mode of this presence: whether being everywhere and in all things through essence, presence, and power is proper to God alone. After distinguishing the modes of being-in (by power, presence, and essence) and of being in place (circumscriptive, definitive, repletive), Biel establishes that God is in all things through power, presence, and essence, and in every place repletively rather than locally. Following Ockham and Scotus against the inference attributed to Aquinas, he denies that God's immediate causality over all things by itself entails his essential omnipresence. He also distinguishes a contingent sense of universal presence, in principle communicable to a creature, from the necessary sense proper to God alone, a conditional necessity by which God cannot exist without being in whatever exists.
claims: God is present in all things by essence, presence, and power, with special and singular grades of indwelling in the saints and in Christ.
God is in every place repletively, without change, circumscription, or local motion, while remaining in himself non-local and atemporal.
God's immediate causal power over all things does not by itself entail his essential omnipresence (with Ockham and Scotus, against the Thomist inference).
Universal presence is proper to God alone only in a necessary, conditional sense; in a contingent sense it could be communicated to a creature.
concepts: repletive vs. circumscriptive and definitive presence

gbs333-d1e5684.summary: Distinction 44, the final distinction of Book II, turns from the causes and nature of sin (treated in the preceding distinctions) to the power to sin itself and its origin. The preamble summarizes Lombard's text in three conclusions: all power to act well or badly is from God; legitimately exercised power must be obeyed while its abuse is to be resisted; and when an inferior power commands against a superior, the superior is to be heeded. The question asks whether the power to sin was granted by God to the rational creature. Biel holds that the power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom. It evidences freedom but does not belong to its essence, since God and the confirmed blessed are free without it. It was therefore conferred by God and is in itself good, though not an unqualified perfection. Against objections drawn from Bonaventure, he insists that the power to sin, as an absolute reality, is simply from God, and that only the privative disorder of sin is not. The objections are answered by distinctions between God's will of good pleasure and his preceptive will, and between positive powers and mere failings, and by arguing that freedom, the power to sin itself, assimilates man to the supremely free God. The distinction, and with it Biel's commentary on Book II, closes with a doxology and explicit.
claims: All power to act well or badly is from God; legitimate power is to be obeyed and its abuse resisted, with superior authority prevailing over inferior.
The power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom, was given by God, and is good in itself, though not a perfectio simpliciter.
Only the privative disorder of sin, not any positive reality in it, is not from God.
Freedom, including the power to sin, assimilates the rational creature to God, and its perfection lies in free conformity to the divine will.
concepts: obedience and resistance to abuse of power

gbs333-aD56.summary: Partial summary of Book I, resting only on the Prologue and Distinction 37 (2 of the book's 49 direct divisions have interpretations; Distinctions 1–36 and 38–48 are not covered). From these two parts, Book I appears as Biel's Ockhamist treatment of God and of theological knowledge of God. The Prologue establishes the epistemic framework. Theology as possessed by wayfarers is not strictly a science, since its principles are believed, though God could by absolute power make some theological truths evident. Our concepts of God in this life are only indistinct, common or composite. Acquired theology is an aggregate of habits with many subjects. It includes both practical and speculative knowledge, distinguished by whether its conclusions direct free action. Distinction 37 applies this framework to the divine presence: God is in all things by essence, presence, and power, repletively and without change, with special and singular indwelling in the saints and in Christ. Following Ockham and Scotus against Aquinas, Biel denies that causal immediacy alone entails essential omnipresence, and he treats universal presence as proper to God only in a conditional, necessary sense. Nothing should be inferred from this summary about the uncovered distinctions, which per the plan Biel gives at the opening of Distinction 1 cover the Trinity in itself (dd. 2–34) and the divine attributes of knowledge, power, and will (dd. 35–48).
claims: (Partial, from the Prologue) Theology in via is not science properly so called, and our knowledge of God is limited to indistinct concepts.
(Partial, from d. 37) God is present in all things by essence, presence, and power, and his causal immediacy does not by itself entail essential omnipresence.

gbs333-d1e4057.summary: Partial summary of Book II, resting only on Distinction 44, the book's final distinction (1 of 44 direct divisions has an interpretation; Distinctions 1–43 are not covered). The covered material shows Book II ending with the power to sin and its origin, after the preceding distinctions (as the d. 44 preamble notes) treated the causes and nature of sin. Biel argues that all power, including the power to sin, is from God. The power to sin is really identical with the will's freedom, and so good in itself though not an unqualified perfection, while only sin's privative disorder is not from God. Freedom assimilates the rational creature to the supremely free God. The summary says nothing about the creation, angels, human nature, grace, and the other topics of the uncovered distinctions.
claims: (Partial, from d. 44) The power to sin is identical with free will, comes from God, and is good in itself; only the disorder of sin is not from God.

gbs333.summary: Partial summary of Gabriel Biel's Collectorium (Epitome and Collectorium on the four books of the Sentences), resting only on the partial summaries of Book I (Prologue and d. 37) and Book II (d. 44); Books III and IV have no interpretations (2 of 4 direct children covered, both themselves partial). As the Praeambulum states, the work is an abridgment of William of Ockham's Sentences teaching, supplemented where Ockham is silent by other doctors consistent with his principles, and organized by Lombard's distinctions with a summary of Lombard's text before the questions. The covered portions show a consistently Ockhamist approach. Theology as wayfarers possess it is not science properly so called, though God by absolute power could make some of its truths evident, and our concepts of God in this life are indistinct. God is present in all things by essence, presence, and power, though causal immediacy does not by itself entail that presence. Free will, which is identical with the power to sin, is God's good gift, with only the privative disorder of sin not from God. These are samples; they do not represent the full scope of the four books.
claims: (Partial) The Collectorium is an epitome of Ockham's Sentences commentary, filled out with other doctors consistent with Ockham's principles.

(Partial) In the covered portions Biel holds that wayfarers' theology is not strictly a science, that God is omnipresent though not merely in virtue of causal immediacy, and that the power to sin, as free will, is from God.
